title: Deadlock with .Result
cards/0/body:
A button handler waits synchronously for an async method. Here's what happens step by step (the numbers are in the code below):

  • 1. The UI thread calls GetDataAsync. The method sends the request synchronously and, at the await, captures the UI thread's context: SynchronizationContext.Current is a DispatcherSynchronizationContext.
  • 2. GetDataAsync returns an unfinished task, and the UI thread blocks on .Result.
  • 3. The response arrives. The continuation (Parse and return) is sent via Post to the UI thread's queue.
  • 4. But the UI thread is stuck on .Result and doesn't process its queue. The continuation won't run until the UI thread is free, and the UI thread won't be free until the task completes.

Each waits for the other: a deadlock. It can happen in any context that lets in only one thread at a time: WPF, WinForms, Unity and classic ASP.NET on .NET Framework (AspNetSynchronizationContext). ASP.NET Core and console apps have no context, so the loop never closes.
cards/1/task: Switch the handler to .Result and drive the program into a hang.
cards/2/q: WPF: the UI thread called GetDataAsync().Result, and the server's response has already arrived. What is the UI thread waiting for now?
cards/2/options/0: For the GetDataAsync task to complete
cards/2/explain: .Result blocks the thread until the task completes. The response is here, but the task isn't complete yet: its continuation hasn't run.
cards/3/q: Same scenario: the UI thread is stuck on .Result, and the server's response has arrived. What is the GetDataAsync task waiting for now?
cards/3/options/0: For the UI thread to run its continuation from the UI queue
cards/3/options/2: For the thread pool to give it a free thread
cards/3/explain: await captured the UI context, so the continuation went to the UI thread's queue. Only the UI thread can run it, and it's blocked.
cards/4/task: Keep .Result, but move the code to a console app. Will it hang?
cards/5/q: Why doesn't the same .Result hang in a console app?
cards/5/options/0: There's no context: a pool thread runs the continuation, not the blocked main thread
cards/5/options/1: A console app runs code faster
cards/5/options/2: In a console app .Result doesn't block the thread
cards/5/explain: SynchronizationContext.Current == null, so await captured nothing, and the continuation doesn't need the thread that's stuck on .Result.
cards/6/body:
In a console app or ASP.NET Core, .Result won't hang, but the thread still sits idle while it waits. On a server that's a pool thread, and under load such threads run out: that's thread-pool starvation, lesson 5.

Blocking on async code is bad everywhere: in a UI it's a deadlock, on a server it's starvation.
cards/7/q: WPF, the handler calls GetDataAsync().Result, and the server answers after one second. Put the events in order.
cards/7/items/0: GetDataAsync sends the request and, at the await, captures the UI context
cards/7/items/1: GetDataAsync returns an unfinished task, and the UI thread blocks on .Result
cards/7/items/2: A second later the response arrives, and the continuation is sent via Post to the UI thread's queue
cards/7/items/3: The continuation never runs: the UI thread is stuck on .Result, a deadlock
cards/7/explain: The chain closes at the last step: the task needs the UI thread, and the UI thread is waiting for the task.
cards/8/q: Where can this deadlock happen? Select all that apply.
cards/8/explain: You need a context that lets in only one thread at a time: Dispatcher, UnitySynchronizationContext, AspNetSynchronizationContext. ASP.NET Core and console apps have no context.
